idiom_name: one procedure per request over a thin data-source gateway, completed by a single database transaction
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write one procedure per request that takes plain parameters, calls a thin data-source gateway (or the database handle itself), and is bracketed by exactly one transaction - begin before the first read that drives a decision, commit once at the end, roll back on any error. Keep presentation out: no parsing or rendering inside the script; the entry point passes data in and renders the result. Group related scripts in one subject-area class/module, or give each script its own class only when scripts must be stored or executed as objects. Factor a subtask into a subprocedure as soon as a second script needs it, and keep the question 'is this still simple enough for scripts?' under review.
code_sketch:
book_room(room_id, from, to):
    begin_transaction()
    room = gateway.find_room_for_update(room_id)
    if not room.is_free(from, to): rollback(); raise NotAvailable
    rate = gateway.rate_for(room, from, to)
    gateway.insert_booking(room_id, from, to, rate)
    commit()                      # one script == one transaction
    return confirmation
pitfalls: Setting the transaction boundary after the first read: the check and the write are then not atomic and two requests can both pass the check.
Letting one script grow into the whole application instead of extracting subprocedures or switching to a Domain Model.
Returning from the middle of a script without rollback, leaving the transaction open on a pooled connection.

Wrong move: treating an inner script's commit as final when it joined the caller's transaction (Spring PROPAGATION_REQUIRED shares one physical transaction) -> the outer rollback silently discards the inner work, or an UnexpectedRollbackException fires at commit -> let the outermost script own the boundary, or give the inner script its own transaction (PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW) when it must survive.

Wrong move: making remote calls (HTTP, e-mail, queue publish) inside the one transaction -> row locks are held for the duration of network latency and a timeout rolls back all the real work -> move external I/O outside the boundary, or record the intent in-transaction and publish after commit.

Wrong move: check-then-write with a plain SELECT followed by an INSERT -> under default isolation two concurrent requests both pass the check and double-book -> lock the row the check reads (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, as in the sketch) or let a unique constraint fail the losing request.
